parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $5  \left|5 x   –   2\right|    –   1    =    14$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First isolate the modulus*

$\begin{gathered} 5 \left| 5 x - 2 \right| & = 15 \\ \left| 5 x - 2 \right| & = 3 \end{gathered}$

> *To obtain the first solution, assume the contents of the modulus brackets are positive and solve*

$\begin{array}{cc}5 x - 2 & = 3 \\ 5 x & = 5\end{array}$

$x=1$** [1]**

> *To obtain the second solution, assume the contents of the modulus brackets are negative*

$\begin{array}{ccc}5 x - 2 & = & - 3 ( or - 5 x + 2 = 3 ) \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *And solve*

$\begin{array}{ccc}5 x & = & - 1\end{array}$

$x=-\frac{1}{5}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The population $P$, in millions, of a country is given by $P=A\timesb^{t}$, where $t$ is the number of years after January 2000 and $A$ and $b$ are constants. In January 2010 the population was 40 million and had increased to 45 million by January 2013.

Show that $b=$1.04 to 2 decimal places and find $A$ to the nearest integer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *In 2010, 10 years have passed, therefore *$t=10$* and we are given *$P=40.$

> *In 2013, 13 years have passed, therefore *$t=13$* and we are given *$P=45.$

> *This means that we can form two equations*

$40=A\timesb^{10}$

$45=A\timesb^{13}$

**[1]**

> *Solving these simultaneously by dividing the second equation by the first gives*

$\frac{45}{40}=b^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Taking the cube root of both sides gives*

$1.04004...=b$

> *Rounding this to two decimal places, as required, gives*

$1.04=b$

**[1]**

> *Substituting this in to the first equation*

$40 = A \times ( 1.04... ) ^{10}$

> *Dividing both sides by *$1.04^{10}$* and rounding to the nearest integer gives*

$A=27$ **[1]**

> *Find *$P$* by substituting *$Q$* into equation (1)*

parts.problemMd:

 $g(x)=9x-5\mathrm{for}x\inℝ$

** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A mathematical model is used to predict the population of an island, $P$, over time, $t$ years.

A plot of $\mathrm{ln}P$ against $\mathrm{ln}t$ gives a straight line that is the **perpendicular bisector **of the points $( 0 , 11 )$ and $( 6 , 7 )$, as shown.

![Graph with x-axis labelled "ln t" and y-axis labelled "ln P." A line with positive gradient is shown which is the perpendicular bisector to the points (0, 11) and (6, 7).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-further-maths-additional-maths-25/algebra-and-functions/logarithmic-and-exponential-functions/assets/001-graph-with-x-axis-labelled-ln-t-and-y-axis-label.png)

Find and simplify a formula for $P$ in terms of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the midpoint of *$( 0 , 11 )$* and *$( 6 , 7 )$

$\begin{gathered} ( \frac{x_{1} + x_{2} }{2} , \frac{y_{1} + y_{2} }{2} ) & = ( \frac{0 + 6}{2} , \frac{11 + 7}{2} ) \\ = ( \frac{6}{2} , \frac{18}{2} ) \\ = ( 3 , 9 ) \end{gathered}$

**[B1]**

> *Find the gradient of the line from *$( 0 , 11 )$* to *$( 6 , 7 )$

$\begin{gathered} \frac{7 - 11}{6 - 0} & = - \frac{4}{6} \\ = - \frac{2}{3} \end{gathered}$

**[M1]**

> *Find the perpendicular gradient (the negative reciprocal)*

$\frac{3}{2}$

**[A1]**

> *Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector (the line through *$( 3 , 9 )$* with gradient *$\frac{3}{2}$*)*

$y - y_{1} = m \left(x - x_{1}\right)$
$y - 9 = \frac{3}{2} ( x - 3 )$
y minus 9 equals 3 over 2 x minus 9 over 2
y equals 3 over 2 x plus 9 over 2

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A quick check of the graph confirms that this line meant to have a positive gradient and a y-intercept between 4 and 6.

> *Substitute in *$y=\mathrm{ln}P$* and *$x=\mathrm{ln}t$

$\mathrm{ln}P=\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{ln}t+\frac{9}{2}$

**[M1]**

> *Make *$P$* the subject by raising both sides to the power *$e$

$P=e^{\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{ln}t+\frac{9}{2}}$

> *Simplify the answer using index and log laws (and that *$e^{\mathrm{ln}...}$* cancel out)*

$P=e^{\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{ln}t}e^{\frac{9}{2}}\,P=e^{\mathrm{ln}t^{\frac{3}{2}}}e^{\frac{9}{2}}\,P=t^{\frac{3}{2}}e^{\frac{9}{2}}\,P=e^{\frac{9}{2}}t^{\frac{3}{2}}$

$P=e^{\frac{9}{2}}t^{\frac{3}{2}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers which round to $P=90.0t^{\frac{3}{2}}$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation $3^{2x+1}+8(3^{x})--3=0$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The trick here is to recognise that *$3^{2} x + 1 = 3^{2} x \times 3^{1} = ( 3^{x} ) ^{2} \times 3$*, so we could rewrite '*$3^{2} x - 1 + 8 ( 3^{x} ) - 3 = 0$*' as *

$3 ( 3^{x} ) ^{2} + 8 ( 3^{x} ) - 3 = 0$

> *Now we can recognise that we have a quadratic equation in '*$3^{x}$*'. If you like, replace '*$3^{x}$*' with a letter, like *$y$

$3y^{2}+8y-3=0$

> *Factorise this*

$( 3 y - 1 ) ( y + 3 ) = 0$

** [1]**

> *And solve to find *$y$* (or *$3^{x}$*)*

$y=\frac{1}{3},y=-3$

> *Remember that a number to the power of something can't be negative therefore*

$3^{x}=\frac{1}{3},3^{x}\neq-3$

**[1]**

> *If necessary, rewrite *$\frac{1}{3}$* as a power of 3*

$3^{x}=3^{-1}$

$x=-1$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve the equation$4\mathrm{log}_{y}2+\mathrm{log}_{2}y=4$ .
parts.solutionMd:
> *We have two logs with different bases so we need to change them to the same base. Here we will change them both to log*<sub>*2*</sub>* but you could also change to log*<sub>*y *</sub>*and then use a similar method with a quadratic equation in log*<sub>*y*</sub>

> *If you don't recognise log*<sub>*2*</sub>*y** as 1/(log*<sub>*y*</sub>*2) then use the change of base rule, *$\mathrm{log}_{x}y=\frac{\mathrm{log}_{a}y}{\mathrm{log}_{a}x}$

$\mathrm{log}_{y}2=\frac{\mathrm{log}_{2}2}{\mathrm{log}_{2}y}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}_{2}y}$

**or writing **$\mathrm{log}_{2}y$** as**** **$\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}_{y}2}$**[1]**

> *Now rewrite the equation in terms of log*<sub>*2*</sub>

$\frac{4}{\mathrm{log}_{2}y}+\mathrm{log}_{2}y=4$

> *Multiply all terms by log*<sub>*2*</sub>*y** to form a quadratic equation in log*<sub>*2*</sub>*y*

$4 + ( log_{2} y ) ^{2} = 4 log_{2} y$

> *If you like, replace log*<sub>*2*</sub>*y** with a letter, like **x**, and rearrange to an equation equalling 0*

$\begin{array}{ccc}4 + x ^{2} & = & 4 x \\ x ^{2} - 4 x + 4 & = 0\end{array}$

> *Factorise and solve*

$\begin{array}{cc}x ^{2} - 4 x + 4 & = 0 \\ ( x - 2 ) ^{2} & = 0 \\ x = 2\end{array}$

> *Remember that **x** = log*<sub>*2*</sub>*y** therefore*

$\begin{array}{cc}log_{2} y & = 2\end{array}$

**or " **$\mathrm{log}_{y}2=\frac{1}{2}$**" using similar method**** [1]**

> *Rewrite in exponent form*

$\begin{array}{rcl} 2^{2} & = y \end{array}$

$y=4$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Write the expression $\mathrm{log}_{a}9+(\mathrm{log}_{a}b)(\mathrm{log}_{\sqrt{b}}9a)$ in the form $c+d\mathrm{log}_{a}9$, where $c$ and $d$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Change the base of *$\mathrm{log}_{\sqrt{b}}9a$* to base *$a$*.*

$\frac{\mathrm{log}_{a}9a}{\mathrm{log}_{a}\sqrt{b}}$

**[1]**

> *Use the logarithm power law to rewrite the denominator.*

$\frac{log_{a} 9 a}{ ( \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} ) log_{a} b}$

> *Use the addition/multiplication law to rewrite the numerator.*

$\frac{log_{a} 9 + log_{a} a}{ ( \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} ) log_{a} b}$

**[1]**

$\mathrm{log}_{a}a=1$

$\frac{ ( log_{a} 9 ) + 1}{ ( \frac{1}{2} ) log_{a} b}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute into original equation.*

$log_{a} 9 + ( log_{a} b ) ( \frac{ ( log_{a} 9 ) + 1}{ ( \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} ) log_{a} b} )$

> *Simplify.*

$log_{a} 9 + ( \frac{ ( log_{a} 9 ) + 1}{ ( \text{begin display style} \frac{1}{2} ) } )$

$log_{a} 9 + 2 ( log_{a} 9 ) + 2$

$2+3\mathrm{log}_{a}9$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the exact solution of $3^{2x}-3^{x+1}-4=0$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Let *$y=3^{x}$* then *

$3^{2x}=3^{x}\times3^{x}=y^{2}$

$3^{x+1}=3^{x}\times3^{1}=3y$

> *Use the original equation and change the variables*

$3^{2x}-3^{x+1}-4=0$

$y^{2}-3y-4=0$

**[1]**

> *Factorise and solve the quadratic equation*

$( y + 1 ) ( y - 4 ) = 0$

$y=-1\mathrm{or}y=4$

**[1]**

> *But *$y=3^{x}$* so*

$3^{x}=-1\mathrm{or}3^{x}=4$

**[1]**

> *Solve each equation using the inverse which is *$\mathrm{log}_{3}$

$x = log_{3} ( - 1 ) or x = log_{3} 4$

> *The first equation has no solutions so disregard this and our final answer is*

$x=\mathrm{log}_{3}4$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Solve the simultaneous equations

$10^{x+2y}=5$,

$10^{3x+4y}=50$ ,

giving $x$ and $y$ in exact simplified form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Taking logs of both sides of each equation*

$\mathrm{lg}10^{x+2y}=\mathrm{lg}5$

$\mathrm{lg}10^{3x+4y}=\mathrm{lg}50$

> $\mathrm{lg}10=1$*, therefore*

$x+2y=\mathrm{lg}5$

$3x+4y=\mathrm{lg}50$

**[1]**

> *Multiplying the first equation by 2 gives*

$2x+4y=2\mathrm{lg}5$

> *Subtracting this from the second equation gives *

$x=\mathrm{lg}50-2\mathrm{lg}5$

**[1]**

> *Using the log laws that *$a\mathrm{log}b=\mathrm{log}b^{a}$* and *$\mathrm{log}m-\mathrm{log}n=\mathrm{log}\frac{m}{n}$

$x=\mathrm{lg}50-\mathrm{lg}25=\mathrm{lg}2$

**[1]**

> *Substituting this into the equation *$x+2y=\mathrm{lg}5$

$\mathrm{lg}2+2y=\mathrm{lg}5$

$2y=\mathrm{lg}\frac{5}{2}$

$x=\mathrm{lg}2,y=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{lg}\frac{5}{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{log}_{a}\sqrt{b}-\frac{1}{2}=\mathrm{log}_{b}a,\mathrm{where}a>0\mathrm{and}b>0$.

Solve this equation for $b$, giving your answers in terms of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
$\mathrm{log}_{a}\sqrt{b}-\frac{1}{2}=\mathrm{log}_{b}a$

> *Rewrite the square root as a power*

$\mathrm{log}_{a}b^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{2}=\mathrm{log}_{b}a$

> *Bring down the *$\frac{1}{2}$* *

$\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{log}_{a}b-\frac{1}{2}=\mathrm{log}_{b}a$

**[1]**

> *Change the base of the log on the right hand side *

$\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{log}_{a}b-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{log}_{a}b}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply through by 2*

$\mathrm{log}_{a}b-1=\frac{2}{\mathrm{log}_{a}b}$

> *Multiply through by *$\mathrm{log}_{a}b$

$( log_{a} b ) ^{2} - log_{a} b = 2$

> *Make the equation equal to 0*

$( log_{a} b ) ^{2} - log_{a} b - 2 = 0$

**[1]**

> *Factorise the quadratic equation*

$( log_{a} b - 2 ) ( log_{a} b + 1 ) = 0$

**[1]**

> *Find the solutions*

*Either* $\mathrm{log}_{a}b=2$ *or *$\mathrm{log}_{a}b=-1$* *

> *Make **b** the subject*

* *$\mathrm{log}_{a}b=2$* leads to *$a^{2}=b$ $\mathrm{log}_{a}b=-1$* leads to *$a^{-1}=b$

$b=a^{2}\mathrm{or}b=\frac{1}{a}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Solve the simultaneous equations.

$log_{3} ( x + y ) = 2$

$2 log_{3} ( x + 1 ) = log_{3} ( y + 2 )$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The first equation is *$log_{3} ( x + y ) = 2$

> *Use the inverse of *$\mathrm{log}_{3}$* which is doing 3 to the power of both sides*

$x+y=3^{2}$

* (1)**      *$x+y=9$

**[1]**

> *The second equation is *$2 log_{3} ( x + 1 ) = log_{3} ( y + 2 )$

> *Move the 2 from in front to be a power*

$log_{3} ( x + 1 ) ^{2} = log_{3} ( y + 2 )$

> *Use the inverse of *$\mathrm{log}_{3}$* which is doing 3 to the power of both sides*

$\left(x + 1\right)^{2}=y+2$

**[1]**

> *Subtract 2 from both sides to make *$y$* the subject *

*(2)  **    *$y=\left(x + 1\right)^{2}-2$

> *Solve equations (1) and (2) simultaneously by substituting equation (2) into equation (1)*

$x + ( x + 1 ) ^{2} - 2 = 9$

**[1]**

> *Expand the double bracket*

$x+x^{2}+x+x+1-2=9$

> *Simplify the left hand side*

$x^{2}+3x-1=9$

> *Subtract 9 from both sides to make the quadratic equal 0*

$x^{2}+3x-10=0$

**[1]**

> *Solve by factorising (or using the quadratic formula)*

$( x + 5 ) ( x - 2 ) = 0$

$x=-5\mathrm{or}x=2$

**[1]**

> *Find *$y$* by substituting each value into equation (1)*

*When *$x=-5$

$y = 9 - ( - 5 ) = 14$

*Reject this as we cannot have* $log_{3} ( - )$

*When* $x=2$

$y=9-2=7$

$x=2\mathrm{and}y=7$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
It is known that $y=A\times10^{bx^{2}}$, where $A$ and $b$ are constants. When $\mathrm{lg}y$ is plotted against $x^{2}$, a straight line passing through the points (3.63, 5.25) and (4.83, 6.88) is obtained.

parts.solutionMd:
$y=A\times10^{bx^{2}}$

$lg y = lg ( A \times 10^{b} x ^{2} )$

> *Use logarithm laws to rewrite.*

$\mathrm{lg}y=\mathrm{lg}A+bx^{2}$

$\mathrm{lg}y=bx^{2}+\mathrm{lg}A$

**[1]**

> *Find the gradient between the two coordinates.*

$m=\frac{6.88-5.25}{4.83-3.63}\,m=1.3583...$

> *  *

> *Substitute *$m=1.36$*, *$X=x^{2}$* and *$y = lg ( y )$* into the equation of a line *$( Y = m X + c )$*.*

> * *

$\mathrm{lg}y=1.358x^{2}+\mathrm{lg}A$

> *Compare to *$\mathrm{lg}y=bx^{2}+\mathrm{lg}A$

$b=1.358$

> *  *

> *Substitute *$b=1.358$* and one of the coordinates into *$Y=mX+c$* to find the value of *$c$*.*

> *  *

> *  *$\begin{gathered} 5.25 & = 1.358 ( 3.63 ) + c \\ \\ c = 0.32046 \end{gathered}$

> *Compare to *$\mathrm{lg}y=bx^{2}+\mathrm{lg}A$

$\mathrm{lg}A=0.32046$

> *Solve by raising 10 to the power of both sides.*

$A=10^{0.32046}\,A=2.0915...$

$A=2.09$* ***[1]**

$b=1.36$* ***[1]**

> *Rearrange the first equation.*

> *Combine using logarithm laws.*

parts.problemMd: Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of the curve $x^{2}+xy=9$ and the line $y=\frac{2}{3}x-2$.

parts.solutionMd:
(i) *To find the expression for velocity, **v,** integrate the expression for acceleration.   *

$\text{integral} ( 6 \text{cos} 2 t ) \mathrm{d} t = 3 \text{sin} 2 t + C$

$v=3\mathrm{sin}2t+C$

$[ 1 ]$

> *To find C, substitute *$t=0$* and *$v=10$* into the equation.*

> *  *

> $10 = 3 sin ( 2 \times 0 ) + C$*  *

> *Simplify, then rearrange, to find C.*

$C=10$

$[ 1 ]$

> *Substitute *$C=10$* into the equation for velocity.*

> $v=3\mathrm{sin}2t+10$* *$[ 1 ]$

ii) *To find the expression for displacement, *$s$*, integrate the expression for velocity.  *

$\text{integral} ( 3 \text{sin} 2 t + 10 ) \mathrm{d} t$

> *Break up the integral.*

$\text{integral} ( 3 \text{sin} 2 t ) \mathrm{d} t + \text{integral} 10 \mathrm{d} t$

> *Integrate *$3\mathrm{sin}2t$* with respect to *$t$*.*

$\text{integral} ( 3 \text{sin} 2 t ) \mathrm{d} t = \frac{ - 3 \text{cos} 2 t}{2} + d$

$= - \frac{3}{2} ( \text{cos} 2 t ) + d$

> *Combine with the integral of 10.*

$s = - \frac{3}{2} ( \text{cos} 2 t ) + 10 t + d$

$[ 1 ]$

> *To find *$d$*, substitute *$s=0$* and *$t=0$* into the equation.*

> *  *

$\begin{array}{cc}0 = & - \frac{3}{2} ( \text{cos} 0 ) + 10 ( 0 ) + d \\ d = & \frac{3}{2}\end{array}$

$[ 1 ]$

> *Substitute *$d=\frac{3}{2}$*into the equation for displacement.*

**Final answer:** $s=-\frac{3}{2}(cos2t)+10t+\frac{3}{2}$** **$[ 1 ]$

parts.problemMd:
A particle, $P$, moves in a straight line such that its displacement from a fixed point at time $t$ is s.

The acceleration of $P$ is given by $( 2 t + 4 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} , \text{for} t > 0$

(i) Given that $P$ has a velocity of 9 when $t=6$, find the velocity of $P$ at time $t$.

(ii) Given that s = $\frac{1}{3}$ when $t=6$, find the displacement of $P$ at time $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
i) *To find the expression for velocity, integrate the expression for acceleration. Integrate using reverse chain rule.*

$\text{integral} ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{d} t = \frac{ ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} half}{1 half} \times \frac{1}{2} + C$

$V = ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half} + C$

$[ 1 ]$

> *To find C, substitute *$t=6$* and *$V=9$* into the equation.*

> $9 = ( 2 ( 6 ) + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half} + C$*  *

> *Simplify, then rearrange, to find C.*

$9=\sqrt{16}+C$

$C=5$

$[ 1 ]$

> *Substitute *$C=5$*into the equation for velocity.*

> $V=(2t+4)^{\frac{1}{2}}+5$* *$[ 1 ]$

ii) *To find the expression for displacement, integrate the expression for velocity.  *

$\text{integral} ( ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half} + 5 ) \mathrm{d} t$

> *Break up the integral.*

$\text{integral} ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half d} t + \text{integral} 5 \mathrm{d} t$

> *Integrate *$5$* with respect to *$t$*.*

`integral 5 space straight d t space equals space 5 t space plus space d`

> *Integrate *$( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half}$* with respect to *$t$* using reverse chain rule.*

$\text{integral} ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{1} \text{half d} t = \frac{ ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} \times \frac{1}{2} + d$

$= \frac{1}{3} ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} + d$

> *Combine both results.*

$s = \frac{1}{3} ( 2 t + 4 ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} + 5 t + d$

$[ 1 ]$

> *To find *$d$*, substitute *$s=\frac{1}{3}$* and *$t=6$* into the equation.*

$\frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{3} ( 2 ( 6 ) + 4 ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} + 5 ( 6 ) + d$

> *Simplify, then rearrange, to find d.*

$\frac{1}{3}=\frac{64}{3}+30+d$

$d=-51$

$[ 1 ]$

> *Substitute *$d=-51$*into the equation for displacement.*

$\frac{1}{3}(2t+4)^{\frac{3}{2}}+5t-51$ $[ 1 ]$

parts.problemMd:
A particle travels along a straight line with a velocity, $v$ ms<sup>-1</sup>, given by

$v = 6 ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{2} + \frac{5}{2}$

for  $t\geq0$ where $t$ is time in seconds. The particle has an initial displacement of $-1$ metres.

Find the acceleration after 2 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate velocity to find acceleration*

**Method 1**

> *Expand and simplify the velocity first*

$\begin{array}{cc}v = & 6 ( t ^{2} - \frac{1}{2} t - \frac{1}{2} t + \frac{1}{4} ) + \frac{5}{2} \\ v = & 6 ( t ^{2} - t + \frac{1}{4} ) + \frac{5}{2} \\ v = & 6 t ^{2} - 6 t + \frac{3}{2} + \frac{5}{2} \\ v = & 6 t ^{2} - 6 t + 4\end{array}$

**[M1]**

> *Then differentiate *$v$* to find *$a$

$a=12t-6$

**[M1 A1]**

> *Substitute in *$t=2$

$a=12\times2-6$

**Final answer:** **18 ms**<sup>**-2**</sup>

**[A1]**

**Method 2**

> *Use the chain rule, *$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{du}\frac{du}{dt}$* where *$u=t-\frac{1}{2}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}v = & 6 u ^{2} + \frac{5}{2} u = t - \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} u} & = & 12 u \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} t} = 1\end{array}$

**[M1]**

> *This gives*

$\begin{array}{cc}a = & 12 u \times 1 \\ a = & 12 ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) \end{array}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **A1:** For an answer at least in the form $k ( t - \frac{1}{2} )$.
> 
> **A1:** For $12 ( t - \frac{1}{2} )$ or $12t-6$.

> *Substitute in *$t=2$

$a = 12 ( 2 - \frac{1}{2} )$

**Final answer:** **18 ms**<sup>**-2**</sup>

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the displacement after 2 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1**

> *Integrate *$v=6t^{2}-6t+4$* to get displacement *$s$* and add a constant of integration*

$s=\frac{6t^{3}}{3}-\frac{6t^{2}}{2}+4t+c$

**[M1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for at least two correct terms in $t$ (can be unsimplified).

> *Simplify*

$s=2t^{3}-3t^{2}+4t+c$

**[A1]**

> *The initial displacement is *$-1$* so substitute in *$s=-1$* when *$t=0$* to find *$c$

$\begin{array}{ccc} - 1 & = & 0 - 0 + 0 + c \\ c = & - 1\end{array}$

> *Substitute this value of *$c$* back into the expression for *$s$

$s=2t^{3}-3t^{2}+4t-1$

**[A1]**

> *Substitute in *$t=2$

$s = 2 ( 2 ) ^{3} - 3 ( 2 ) ^{2} + 4 ( 2 ) - 1$

**Final answer:** **11  m**

**[A1]**

**Method 2**

> *Integrate *$v = 6 ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{2} + \frac{5}{2}$* using *$\text{integral} ( a x + b ) ^{n} \mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{a} \times \frac{1}{n + 1} ( a x + b ) ^{n} + 1 + c$* to get displacement *$s$* *

> *Add a constant of integration*

$s = 6 \times \frac{1}{1} \times \frac{1}{3} ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + \frac{5}{2} t + c$

**[M1 A1]**

> *Simplify*

$s = 2 ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + \frac{5}{2} t + c$

> *The initial displacement is *$-1$* so substitute in *$s=-1$* when *$t=0$* to find *$c$

$\begin{array}{ccc} - 1 & = & 2 ( 0 - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + 0 + c \\ - 1 & = & - \frac{1}{4} + c \\ c = & - \frac{3}{4}\end{array}$

> *Substitute this value of *$c$* back into the expression for *$s$

$s = 2 ( t - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + \frac{5}{2} t - \frac{3}{4}$

**[A1]**

> *Substitute in *$t=2$

$s = 2 ( 2 - \frac{1}{2} ) ^{3} + \frac{5}{2} ( 2 ) - \frac{3}{4}$

**Final answer:** **11  m**

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

parts.solutionMd:

**[1]**

> *Taking natural log of both sides of the first solution gives*

$t=\mathrm{ln}6(\mathrm{seconds})$  **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Given that $y=\mathrm{tan}x$, use calculus to find the approximate change in $y$ as $x$ increases from $-\frac{π}{4}$ to $h-\frac{π}{4}$, where $h$ is small.
parts.solutionMd:

> *Differentiate *$y=\mathrm{tan}x$*.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{sec}^{2}x$

**[1]**

> *Substituting *$x=-\frac{π}{4}$* into *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* gives the gradient at of*$f$* at *$x=-\frac{π}{4}$*.*

$x = - \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{4} , \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \sec ^{2} ( - \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{4} )$

**[1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the $x$-coordinate of the stationary point on the curve $y = ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) x^{2} + x - 1$, giving your answer in the form $a+b\sqrt{3}$,where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate *$y$* with respect to *$x$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) x + 1$

**[1]**

> *Stationary points are where *$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$*.*

$2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) x + 1 = 0$

> *Rearrange to find *$x$*.*

$2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) x = - 1$

$x = - \frac{1}{2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )}$

> *Rationalise the denominator.*

$\begin{gathered} x = - \frac{1}{2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} )} \\times \frac{( 2 + \sqrt{3} )}{( 2 + \sqrt{3} )} \\ x = - \frac{2 + \sqrt{3} }{2 ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) ( 2 + \sqrt{3} )} \\ x = - \frac{2 + \sqrt{3} }{2 ( 4 - 3 )} \\ x = - \frac{2 + \sqrt{3} }{2} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$x=-1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: The radius, $r\mathrm{cm}$, of a circle is increasing at the rate of $5\mathrm{cms}^{--1}$. Find, in terms of $π$, the rate at which the area of the circle is increasing when $r=3$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a connected rates of change question - the rate of change of the radius is connected to the rate of change of the area.*

> *The radius of the circle is increasing with respect to time.*

$\frac{dr}{dt}=5$

**[1]**

> *To find the rate at which the area is increasing, use chain rule.*

$\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{dr}{dt}\times\frac{dA}{dr}$

> *The area of a circle is given by *$A=πr^{2}$*, so,*

$\frac{dA}{dr}=2πr$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the two results into chain rule.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = 5 \\times 2 \mathrm{\pi } r \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = 10 \mathrm{\pi } r \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the given value of **r.*

$\frac{dA}{dt}=10π\times3$

$\frac{dA}{dt}=30π\mathrm{cm}^{2}s^{-1}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: The volume, $V$, of a sphere of radius $r$ is given by $V=\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{πr}^{3}$. The radius, $r\mathrm{cm}$, of a sphere is increasing at the rate of $0.5\mathrm{cms}^{-1}$. Find, in terms of $π$, the rate of change of the volume of the sphere when $r=0.25$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We know that the radius is increasing at a rate of 0.5*$\mathrm{cms}^{-1}$*.*

$\frac{dr}{dt}=0.5$

**[1]**

> *Differentiate the volume of the sphere with respect to **r.*

$\frac{dV}{dr}=3\times\frac{4}{3}πr^{2}$

$\frac{dV}{dr}=4πr^{2}$

**[1]**

> *We want to find the rate of change of the volume which is *$\frac{dV}{dt}$* so use the chain rule.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = \frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} r} \\times \frac{ \mathrm{d} r}{ \mathrm{d} t} \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = 4 \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} \\times 0.5 \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = 2 \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Find *$\frac{dV}{dt}$* when *$r=\frac{1}{4}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} t} = 2 \mathrm{\pi } \\times ( 1 \frac{1}{4} )^{2} = \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{8} $

$\frac{π}{8}\mathrm{cm}^{3}s^{-1}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Given that $y = ( x ^{2} - 1 ) \sqrt{5 x + 2}$, show that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{Ax^{2}+Bx+C}{2\sqrt{5x+2}}$, where $A,B$ and $C$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the product rule, *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( u v ) = u \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} + v \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x}$*, and the chain rule.*

*Let *$u=x^{2}-1$* and *$v = ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{1} \text{half}$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( ( x ^{2} - 1 ) \times \frac{1}{2} ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} \times 5 ) + ( ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{1} \text{half} \times 2 x )$

**for **$\frac{5}{2}(5x+2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$**[1]**

**for differentiation of a product**** [1]**

**fully correct differentiation ****[1]**

> *Simplify each bracket.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( \frac{5}{2} ( x ^{2} - 1 ) ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} ) + ( 2 x ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{1} \text{half} )$

> *Take out common factor of *$\frac{1}{2} ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{1}{2} ( 5 x + 2 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} ( 5 ( x ^{2} - 1 ) + 4 x ( 5 x + 2 ) )$

**[1]**

> *Expand and simplify, writing as a fraction.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5x^{2}-5+20x^{2}+8x}{2\sqrt{5x+2}}$

> *Simplify.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{25x^{2}+8x-5}{2\sqrt{5x+2}}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The equation of a curve is $y=x\sqrt{16-x^{2}}\mathrm{for}0\leqx\leq4$.

Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point of the curve.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Stationary points occur when *$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$* so first differentiate using the product rule, for *$y=uv,\frac{dy}{dx}=v\frac{du}{dx}+u\frac{dv}{dx}$*.*

$u = x v = ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$

$\frac{du}{dx}=1$

$\frac{d v}{d x} = \frac{1}{2} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} \times - 2 x = - x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Apply the product rule.*

$\frac{d y}{d x} = ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half} \times 1 + x \times ( - x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} )$

** ****use product rule ****[1] **
**fully correct ****[1]**

> *Simplify and set equal to 0.*

$0 = ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half} - x ^{2} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Adding *$x ^{2} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$* to both sides gives.*

$x ^{2} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} = ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$

$x \frac{ ^{2} }{open} \text{parentheses} 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half} = ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$

> *Multiplying both sides by *$( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$*.*

$x^{2}=16-x^{2}$

> *Adding *$x^{2}$* to both sides.*

$2x^{2}=16$

$x^{2}=8$

**[1]**

> *Finding the square root of both sides - disregard the negative root as it's outside the range given in the question.*

$x=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$

> *Substituting this into the equation gives the y co-ordinate.*

$y=8$

$(2\sqrt{2},8)$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Find $\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}}$and hence evaluate the area enclosed by the curve $y=x\sqrt{16-x^{2}}$ and the lines $y=0,x=1\mathrm{and}x=3$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiating using the chain rule that states that *$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{du}{dx}\times\frac{dy}{du}$

> $y=u^{\frac{3}{2}}$*           *$u=16-x^{2}$

$\frac{dy}{du}=\frac{3}{2}u^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{du}{dx}=-2x$

> *Substituting into the chain rule gives*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=-2x\times\frac{3}{2}u^{\frac{1}{2}}$

** ****attempt at chain rule ****[1]**

> *Substituting in the expression for *$u$

$\frac{d y}{d x} = - 2 x \times \frac{3}{2} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$

**[1]**

> *Simplifying gives*

$\frac{d y}{d x} = - 3 x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$

> *The area required is*

$integral_{1}^{3} x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half} d x$

> *You have just differentiated *$( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}}$* to get *$- 3 x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half}$*, which is almost what you are being asked to integrate to find the area. The area is minus-a-third of the result above, so you can write down*

$\int_{1}^{3} x ( 16 - x^{2} )^{1 \frac{1}{2}} d x = [ - 1 \frac{1}{3} ( 16 - x^{2} )^{ \frac{3}{2} } ]_{1}^{3}$

** ****for **$-\frac{1}{3}$**[1]**

**for **$k ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}}$** [1]**

> *Applying the limits*

$( - \frac{1}{3} ( 16 - 3 ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} ) - ( - \frac{1}{3} ( 16 - 1 ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} )$

$13.2$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A curve has equation $y=(2x-1)\sqrt{4x+3}$.

Show that $\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{4 ( A x + B ) }{\sqrt{4 x + 3}}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate *$y = ( 2 x - 1 ) \sqrt{4 x + 3}$* using the product rule and chain rule.*

> $u=2x-1$*    *$v = ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{1} \text{half}$

> $\frac{du}{dx}=2$*    *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$** ****[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( 2 ) ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{1} \text{half} + ( 2 x - 1 ) ( 2 ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} )$

**use of product rule ****[1]**
* ***all terms correct ****[1]**

> *Simplify - start by taking factors of *$2$* and *$( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} [ 4 x + 3 + 2 x - 1 ]$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} [ 6 x + 2 ]$

> *Rewrite as a fraction.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( \frac{2}{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x + 3 ) ^{1} \text{half} ) ( 6 x + 2 )$

> *Multiply the fractions.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{12 x + 4}{ ( 4 x + 3 ) ^{begin} \text{display style} 1 half}$

> *Factorise the numerator, and rewrite the denominator to express as required.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4(3x+1)}{\sqrt{4x+3}}$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=x^{3}-6x^{2}+3x+10$ at the point where $x=1$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute *$x=1$* into the equation to find the *$y$*-coordinate.*

$y = 1 ^{3} - 6 ( 1 ) ^{2} + 3 ( 1 ) + 10$

$y=8$

**[1]**

> *Differentiate the equation of the curve to find the gradient function.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}-12x+3$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 3 ( 1 ) ^{2} - 12 ( 1 ) + 3$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=-6$

**[1]**

*Find the equation of the tangent with point *$( 1 , 8 )$* and gradient *$-6$.

$y=-6x+14$

$y=-6x+14$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve y = x³ - 6x² + 3x + 10 at the point where x = 1.

The equation of the tangent is y = -6x + 14

Find the coordinates of the point where this tangent meets the curve again.
parts.solutionMd:
> *From part (a), the equation of the tangent is *$y=-6x+14$*. Equate the tangent and the curve.*

$-6x+14=x^{3}-6x^{2}+3x+10$

> *Rearrange to get a cubic equation.*

$\begin{array}{cc}14 = & x ^{3} - 6 x ^{2} + 9 x + 10 \\ x ^{3} - 6 x ^{2} + 9 x - 4 & = 0\end{array}$

**[1]**

> *From part (a) we know *$x=1$* is a solution.*

$\left(x - 1\right)$* is a factor of the cubic*

**[1]**

> *Factorise the cubic using long division (or inspection).*

`long division by x minus 1 yields none none none none 1 x squared none minus 5 x none plus 4 pile 1 x cubed none minus 6 x squared none plus 9 x none minus 4 1 x cubed none minus 1 x squared none plus 0 x none plus 0 none minus horizontal line none none none negative 5 x squared none plus 9 x none minus 4 none none none negative 5 x squared none plus 5 x none plus 0 none minus horizontal line none none none none none none none none 4 x none minus 4 none none none none none none none none 4 x none minus 4 none minus horizontal line none none none none none none none none none none none none 0 end pile end long division`

> *The factorised cubic is*

$( x - 1 ) ( x ^{2} - 5 x + 4 ) = 0$

**[1]**

> *Factorise the second bracket.*

$( x - 1 ) ( x - 1 ) ( x - 4 ) = 0$

**[1]**

> $\left(x - 1\right)$* is a repeated factor and is the solution we already know from part (a). The other solution will give us the *$x$*-coordinate of where the tangent meets the curve again.*

$x-4=0$

$x=4$

> *Substitute *$x=4$* into the equation of the tangent to find the *$y$*-coordinate.*

$y = - 6 ( 4 ) + 14 = - 10$

**The tangent and curve meet again at the point**** **$(4,-10)$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$
parts.solutionMd:
*To differentiate *$y = ln ( 1 + \text{sin} x )$, *we can use the fact that the differential of *$\mathrm{ln}x$* is *$\frac{1}{x}$* and chain rule.*

$\frac{1}{1+\mathrm{sin}x}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

It is given that y = ln(1 + sin x) for 0 < x < π.

Find dy/dx

To differentiate y = ln(1 + sin x), we can use the fact that the differential of ln x is 1/x and chain rule.

dy/dx = 1/(1 + sin x) × cos x

dy/dx = (cos x)/(1 + sin x)

Find the value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ when $x=\frac{π}{6}$, giving your answer in the form $\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}$, where $a$ is an integer.
parts.solutionMd:
*From part (**a)**, we know that* $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\mathrm{cos}x}{1+\mathrm{sin}x}$.

*Substitute* $x=\frac{π}{6}$ *into *$\frac{dy}{dx}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ \text{cos} ( \frac{pi}{6} ) }{1 + \text{sin} ( \frac{pi}{6} ) }$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} ) }{\frac{3}{2}}$
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$

> *Rewrite in the form as specified in the question.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

It is given that y = ln(1 + sin x) for 0 < x < π.

Find dy/dx

dy/dx = cos x / (1 + sin x)

Find the values of $x$ for which $\frac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{tan}x$.
parts.solutionMd:
*From part (a), we know that *$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\mathrm{cos}x}{1+\mathrm{sin}x}$. *Equate to *$\mathrm{tan}x$* to form a trigonometric equation.*

$\frac{\mathrm{cos}x}{1+\mathrm{sin}x}=\mathrm{tan}x$

> *Use *$\mathrm{tan}x=\frac{\mathrm{sin}x}{\mathrm{cos}x}$* to simplify.*

$\frac{\mathrm{cos}x}{1+\mathrm{sin}x}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}x}{\mathrm{cos}x}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange.*

$\frac{ \text{cos} x}{1 + \text{sin} x} \times \text{cos} x = \text{sin} x$
$cos ^{2} x = ( 1 + sin x ) sin x$
cos squared space x equals sin space x plus sin squared space x

> *Use *$\mathrm{cos}^{2}x=1-\mathrm{sin}^{2}x$* to make the equation in terms of *$\mathrm{sin}x$* only.*

$\begin{array}{ccc}1 - \text{sin} ^{2} x & = & \text{sin} x + \text{sin} ^{2} x\end{array}$

> *Rearrange.*

$2\mathrm{sin}^{2}x+\mathrm{sin}x-1=0$

**[1]**

> *Factorise this quadratic equation and solve.*

$( 2 \text{sin} x - 1 ) ( \text{sin} x + 1 ) = 0$

$\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{1}{2},\mathrm{sin}x=-1$

$\mathrm{sin}x=-1$* has no solutions in the range *$0<x<π$. $\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{1}{2}$* has two solutions in the range *$0<x<π$*.*

> $\text{sin} ^{ - } 1 ( \frac{1}{2} ) = \frac{pi}{6}$* *

> *Considering the graph of *$y=\mathrm{sin}x$* or using *$\sin ( \mathrm{\pi } - x ) = \sin x$*, the second solution can be found.*

$π-\frac{π}{6}=\frac{5π}{6}$

$x=\frac{π}{6}$* and *$x=\frac{5π}{6}$** [2]*** *
**1 mark for each**

parts.problemMd:

$y=x-2π$* ***[1]**

**[1]**

> *Divide this by -1 to find *$m$*, the gradient of the normal.*

$m=\frac{-1}{-\frac{3}{20}}=\frac{20}{3}$

**[1]**

> *Find *$y$* when *$x=-5$*.*

**[1]**

> *Substitute *$( - 5 , ln 20 )$* and *$m=\frac{20}{3}$* into the equation of a straight line. Here we will use the point-gradient form, *$y - y_{1} = m \left(x - x_{1}\right)$*.*

$y - ln 20 = \frac{20}{3} ( x - ( - 5 ) )$

 **Equivalent forms of the equation are acceptable**

$\begin{array}{ccc}0 - ln 20 & = & \frac{20}{3} \text{stretchy} ( x + 5 \text{stretchy} ) \\ - ln 20 \div \frac{20}{3} & = & x + 5 \\ \frac{ - 3 ln 20}{20} - 5 & = x \\ x = & - 5.44935984...\end{array}$

parts.problemMd: The tangent to the curve $y = ln ( 3 x ^{2} - 4 ) - x \frac{ ^{3} }{6}$, at the point where $x=2$, meets the $y$-axis at the point $P$. Find the exact coordinates of $P$.

A container is a circular cylinder, open at one end, with a base radius of $r$ cm and a height of $h$ cm. The volume of the container is 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>. Given that $r$ and $h$ can vary and that the total outer surface area of the container has a minimum value, find this value.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of a cylinder is *$V=πr^{2}h$*.*

$1000=πr^{2}h$

> *Find *$h$* in terms of *$r$*.*

$h=\frac{1000}{πr^{2}}$

**[1]**

> *The cylinder is open at one end so its surface area is *$S=πr^{2}+2πrh$*, so substitute *$h$* into this so the surface area is in terms of *$r$* only.*

$S=πr^{2}+2πr\frac{1000}{πr^{2}}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$S=πr^{2}+\frac{2000}{r}$

**[1]**

> *Differentiate in order to find the minimum surface area.  First, rewrite *$S$* as powers of *$r$*.*

$S=πr^{2}+2000r^{-1}$

$\frac{dS}{dr}=2πr-2000r^{-2}$

**[1]**

> *When the surface area is at its minimum, *$\frac{dS}{dr}=0$*.*

$\frac{dS}{dr}=2πr-2000r^{-2}=0$

**[1]**

> *Solve to find *$r$*.*

$2πr-\frac{2000}{r^{2}}=0$

> *Multiply through by *$r^{2}$*.*

$\begin{gathered} 2 \mathrm{\pi } r^{3} - 2000 & = 0 \\ 2 \mathrm{\pi } r^{3} & = 2000 \\ r = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{1000}{\mathrm{\pi }} } \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute this value into the formula for *$S$*.*

$\begin{gathered} S = \mathrm{\pi } ( \sqrt[3]{ \frac{1000}{\mathrm{\pi }} } )^{2} + \frac{2000}{( \sqrt[3]{ \frac{1000}{\mathrm{\pi }} } )} \\ S = 439.377 566 ... \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

**The minimum surface area is **$439\mathrm{cm}^{2}$** ****(3 s.f.)**** ****[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of the cuboid is*

$4x^{2}h=40$

> *Write *$h$* in terms of *$r$*.*

$x^{2}h=10$

$h=\frac{10}{x^{2}}$

**[1]**

> *The surface area of the cuboid is*

$S = 2 ( 4 x ^{2} ) + thin 2 x h + thin 2 ( 4 x h )$

$S=8x^{2}+10xh$

$S \text{thin} = 8 x ^{2} + 10 x ( \frac{10}{x} ^{2} )$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$S=8x^{2}+\frac{100}{x}$

> *Differentiate *$S$* to find the minimum value but first rewrite as powers of *$x$*.*

$\begin{array}{ccc}S = & 8 x ^{2} + 100 x^{ - } 1 \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} S}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = & 16 x - 100 x^{ - } 2 \\ \frac{d S}{d x} & = & 16 x - \frac{ 100}{x ^{2} }\end{array}$

$S = 8 ( \sqrt[3]{\frac{25}{4}} ) ^{2} + \frac{ 100}{\sqrt[3]{\frac{25}{4}}}$

$81.4\mathrm{cm}^{2}(3s.f)$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

$It is \text{given that} y = \frac{ \text{tan} 3 x}{ \text{sin} x}.$

Find the exact value of ( d y)/( d x) when x = pi / 3.

Given that $x$ is increasing at the rate of 3 units per second, find the corresponding rate of change in $y$ when $x=\frac{π}{3}$ , giving your answer in its simplest surd form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a connected rates of change question, so use chain rule.*

$\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\times\frac{dx}{dt}$

> *The question states that *$x$* is increasing at the rate of 3 units per second.*

$\frac{dx}{dt}=3$

> *From part (a), at *$x=\frac{π}{3}$*.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=2\sqrt{3}$

**[1]**

$\therefore\frac{dy}{dt}=2\sqrt{3}\times3$

$\frac{dy}{dt}=6\sqrt{3}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
It is given that $y=\mathrm{ln}(\mathrm{sin}x+3\mathrm{cos}x)\mathrm{for}0<x<\frac{π}{2}$.

Find $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use chain rule to differentiate *$ln ( f ( x ) )$*. *

$\frac{d y}{d x} = \frac{1}{ ( \text{sin} x + 3 \text{cos} x ) } \times ( \text{cos} x - 3 \text{sin} x )$

**differentiating ln**** [1] **
**chain rule**** [1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\mathrm{cos}x-3\mathrm{sin}x}{\mathrm{sin}x+3\mathrm{cos}x}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

y = ln(sin x + 3 cos x) for 0 < x < π/2

dy/dx = (cos x - 3 sin x)/(sin x + 3 cos x)

Find the value of $x$ for which $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Set *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* from part (a) equal to *$-\frac{1}{2}$*.*

$-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{cos}x-3\mathrm{sin}x}{\mathrm{sin}x+3\mathrm{cos}x}$

> *Multiply both sides by the denominators.*

$- ( \text{sin} x + \text{thin} 3 \text{cos} x ) = 2 \text{cos} x - 6 \text{sin} x$

> *Expand the brackets.*

$-\mathrm{sin}x-3\mathrm{cos}x=2\mathrm{cos}x-6\mathrm{sin}x$

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms.*

$5\mathrm{sin}x=5\mathrm{cos}x$

> *Dividing both sides by *$5\mathrm{cos}x$* and using the identity *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}x}{\mathrm{cos}x}=\mathrm{tan}x$*.*

$\mathrm{tan}x=1$

**[1]**

> *Solving for *$x$* using the range given in part (a).*

$x=\frac{π}{4}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Given that $y=\frac{e^{2x-3}}{x^{2}+1}$, find $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate the equation using the quotient rule and chain rule.*

$u=e^{2x-3}$*    *$v=x^{2}+1$* *

$\frac{du}{dx}=2e^{2x-3}$*  *$\frac{dv}{dx}=2x$*  *

> *Substitute into the quotient rule, *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( v ) ( \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} ) - ( u ) ( \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} ) }{v ^{2} }$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ( 2 \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) - ( 2 x ) ( \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) }{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ^{2} }$

$2e^{2x-1}$** ****[1] **
**[1]**

> *Split into two fractions and simplify.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ( 2 \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) }{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ^{2} } - \frac{ ( 2 x ) ( \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) }{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ^{2} }$

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2e^{2x-3})}{(x^{2}+1)}-\frac{(2xe^{2x-3})}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

$Given \text{that} y = \frac{ \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3}{x ^{2} + 1}, \text{find} \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x}.$

Differentiate the equation using the quotient rule and chain rule.

$u = \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 v = x ^{2} + 1$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 x$

Substitute into the quotient rule, ( d y)/( d x) = (( v ) ( ( d u)/( d x) ) - ( u ) ( ( d v)/( d x) ))/(v ^2).

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ( 2 \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) - ( 2 x ) ( \mathrm{e} ^{2} x - 3 ) }{ ( x ^{2} + 1 ) ^{2} }$

Hence, given that $y$ is increasing at the rate of 2 units per second, find the exact rate of change of $x$ when $x=2$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a connected rates of change question, so we shall need chain rule.*

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}\times\frac{dy}{dt}$

> $y$* is increasing at a rate of 2 units per second, i.e. *$\frac{dy}{dt}=2$*. Substitute *$x=2$* into the equation for*$\frac{dy}{dx}$* from part (a).*

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = & \frac{2 \mathrm{e} ^{2} \times 2 - 3}{2 ^{2} + 1} - \frac{2 \times 2 \times \mathrm{e} ^{2} \times 2 - 3}{ ( 2 ^{2} + 1 ) ^{2} } \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = & \frac{2 \mathrm{e} }{5} - \frac{4 \mathrm{e} }{25} \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = & \frac{6 \mathrm{e} }{25}\end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Keep this in terms of e as the question asks for an exact answer. Substitute into chain rule and solve for *$\frac{dt}{dx}$*.*

$\frac{6e}{25}=\frac{dt}{dx}\times2\,\frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{6e}{50}$

> *We want to find *$\frac{dx}{dt}$* so we need the reciprocal of *$\frac{dt}{dx}$*.*

$\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{50}{6e}$

$\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{25}{3e}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A sphere of radius $r$ cm and volume $V$ cm<sup>3</sup>  is increasing in size with time $t$ seconds. The volume increases at a constant rate of 24 cm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>.

Find the exact rate at which the radius is increasing when the sphere reaches a volume of $\frac{32π}{3}$ cm<sup>3</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of a sphere is given in the exam*

$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$

> *This question requires connect rates of change (an application of the chain rule)*

$\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\times\frac{dr}{dt}$

> *Find *$\frac{dV}{dr}$* by differentiating *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} r} & = \frac{4}{3} \pi ( 3 r^{2} ) \\ = 4 \pi r^{2} \end{gathered}$

**[B1]**

> *You know *$\frac{dV}{dt}=24$* from the question *

> *Substitute *$\frac{dV}{dt}=24$* and *$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} r} & = & 4 pi r ^{2} \end{array}$* into *$\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\times\frac{dr}{dt}$

$24=4πr^{2}\times\frac{dr}{dt}$

**[M1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for using a correct connected rate formula, e.g.  $\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dr}\times\frac{dr}{dt}$ or $\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{dr}{dV}\times\frac{dV}{dt}$, with at least one correct substitution into the formula.

> *The question wants you to find *$\frac{dr}{dt}$* so make *$\frac{dr}{dt}$* the subject*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} r}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = \frac{24}{4 \pi r^{2}} \\ = \frac{6}{\pi r^{2}} \end{gathered}$

> *You need the value of *$\frac{dr}{dt}$* when *$V=\frac{32π}{3}$* but *$\frac{dr}{dt}$* is in terms of *$r$* not *$V$

> *Use *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$* to find *$r$* when *$V=\frac{32π}{3}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{32 pi}{3} & = & \frac{4}{3} pi r ^{3} \\ 32 pi & = & 4 pi r ^{3} \\ 8 = & r ^{3} \\ r = 2\end{array}$

**[A1]**

> *Substitute *$r=2$* into *$\frac{dr}{dt}$

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} r}{ \mathrm{d} t} & = \frac{6}{\pi ( 2 )^{2}} \\ = \frac{6}{4 \pi } \\ = \frac{3}{2 \pi } \end{gathered}$

> *The units are cm for *$r$* and seconds for *$t$*, so cm/s for *$\frac{dr}{dt}$

**Final answer:** $\frac{3}{2π}$** cm s**<sup>**-1**</sup>

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct exact value gets this mark, even without the units.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Be careful: not all questions forgive units (for example, questions that ask for answers in different units or ask for an interpretation).

parts.problemMd:
A sector from a circle of radius $r$ has an internal angle of $θ$ radians, as shown below.

![Diagram of a sector with radius r, central angle θ radians, and the arc forming a part of a circle. Lines are marked to indicate the radius.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-further-maths-additional-maths-25/calculus/differentiation/assets/001-diagram-of-a-sector-with-radius-r-central-angle-.png)

The perimeter of the sector is 4 units and the area of the sector is $A$ square units.

Show that $A = \frac{8 \theta }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} }$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the length of the arc in radians is *$rθ$

> *Find an expression for the total perimeter and set it equal to 4*

$\begin{gathered} r + r \theta + r & = 4 \\ 2 r + r \theta & = 4 \textcircled{1} \end{gathered}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for any correct perimeter equation that uses 4 and $rθ$.

> *The formula for the area of the arc in radians is *$\frac{1}{2}r^{2}θ$

> *Find an expression for the area *$A$

$A = 1 \frac{1}{2} r^{2} \theta \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \textcircled{2} \end{gathered}$

> *Eliminate *$r$*, e.g. make *$r$* the subject of equation 1 by first factorising it out*

$\begin{array}{cc}r ( 2 + \theta ) & = 4 \\ r = & \frac{4}{2 + \theta }\end{array}$

**[M1]**

> *Then substitute this into equation 2*

$A = \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{4}{2 + \theta } ) ^{2} \times \theta$

> *Simplify*

$A = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{16}{open} \text{parentheses} 2 + \theta ) ^{2} \times \theta$

$A = \frac{8 \theta }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} }$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The last mark is for showing the steps that get you from the substitution of $r$ into $A$ to the answer given (not for writing out the "show that" answer).

parts.problemMd: Show that $\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } = \frac{p ( q - \theta ) }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3} }$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To differentiate *$A = \frac{8 \theta }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} }$* you need the quotient rule*

> *Substitute *$u=8θ$* and *$v = ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2}$* into *$\frac{dA}{dθ}=\frac{v\frac{du}{dx}-u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^{2}}$

> *You can use the chain rule to differentiate *$v = ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2}$* (or expand the brackets then differentiate)*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = 2 ( 2 + \theta )^{1} \\times 1 \\ = 2 ( 2 + \theta ) \end{gathered}$

> *The quotient rule gives*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } = \frac{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} ( 8 ) - 8 \theta \times 2 ( 2 + \theta ) }{ [ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} ] ^{2} }$

**[M1 A1]**

> *Factorise out a *$( 2 + \theta )$* from top and bottom of the fraction, then cancel*

`| ( d A)/( d theta) | = (8 ( 2 + theta ) ^2 - 16 theta ( 2 + theta ))/(( 2 + theta ) ^ 4) | | _ = (( 2 + theta ) [ 8 ( 2 + theta ) - 16 theta ])/(( 2 + theta ) ^ 4) | | _ = (/ ( 2 + theta ) [ 8 ( 2 + theta ) - 16 theta ])/(( 2 + theta ) ^ / 4 ^3) | | _ = (8 ( 2 + theta ) - 16 theta)/(( 2 + theta ) ^3) | |`

> *Write this in the form *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } = \frac{p ( q - \theta ) }{ ( \theta + 2 ) ^{3} }$* by simplifying and factorising the numerator*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } & = \frac{16 + 8 \theta - 16 \theta }{( 2 + \theta )^{3}} \\ = \frac{16 - 8 \theta }{( 2 + \theta )^{3}} \\ = \frac{8 ( 2 - \theta )}{( 2 + \theta )^{3}} \end{gathered}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } & = & \frac{8 ( 2 - \theta ) }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3} }\end{array}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the maximum area of the sector. You must show that this area is a maximum.
parts.solutionMd:
> *For the area to be at its maximum point, *$\frac{dA}{dθ}=0$

$\begin{array}{cc}\frac{8 ( 2 - \theta ) }{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3} } & = 0\end{array}$

> *This means the numerator must be equal to zero (then solve for *$θ$*)*

$\begin{array}{cc}8 ( 2 - \theta ) & = 0 \\ \theta = 2\end{array}$

**[B1]**

> *This is the angle, not the area, so substitute *$θ=2$* into *$A$

$\begin{gathered} A = \frac{8 \\times 2}{( 2 + 2 )^{2}} \\ = \frac{16}{4^{2}} \\ = 1 \end{gathered}$

**[B1]**

> *This area, *$A=1$*, could be a maximum area or a minimum area*

**Method 1**

> *You can use a second-derivative test to show it is a maximum area*

> *Substitute *$u = 8 ( 2 - \theta ) = 16 - 8 \theta$* and *$v = ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3}$* into the quotient rule (using the chain rule to find *$\frac{dv}{dx}$*)*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta ^{2} } = \frac{ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3} ( - 8 ) - 8 ( 2 - \theta ) \times 3 ( 2 + \theta ) ^{2} \times 1}{ [ ( 2 + \theta ) ^{3} ] ^{2} }$

> *No major simplifying is needed as you can now substitute *$θ=2$*into the messy result and check the sign*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d}^{2} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta ^{2}} & = \frac{( 2 + 2 )^{3} ( - 8 ) - 8 \\times 0}{[ ( 2 + 2 )^{3} ]^{2}} \\ = \frac{4^{3} ( - 8 )}{( 4^{3} )^{2}} \\ = - \frac{8}{4^{3}} < 0 \end{gathered}$

> *The second derivative is negative at *$θ=2$* so *$A=1$* is a maximum area*

**Final answer:** **The area of 1 square unit is a maximum area as **$\frac{d^{2}A}{dθ^{2}}<0$** at **$θ=2$

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** For attempting to find the second derivative using the quotient rule.
> 
> **A1: **For correctly showing that the second derivative is negative at $θ=2$ (no formal conclusion sentence needed).

**Method 2**

> *You can use a gradient test either side of *$θ=2$* to show it is a maximum area*

> *Substitute, for example, *$θ=1.9$* into *$\frac{dA}{dθ}$* and just look at its sign (no big simplifications are needed)*

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } & = & \frac{8 ( 2 - 1.9 ) }{ ( 2 + 1.9 ) ^{3} } = \frac{8 \times 0.1}{ ( 3.9 ) ^{3} } > 0\end{array}$

> *Substitute, for example, *$θ=2.1$* into *$\frac{dA}{dθ}$* and again just look at its sign*

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} A}{ \mathrm{d} \theta } & = & \frac{8 ( 2 - 2.1 ) }{ ( 2 + 2.1 ) ^{3} } = \frac{8 \times ( - 0.1 ) }{ ( 4.1 ) ^{3} } = - \frac{8 \times 0.1}{ ( 4.1 ) ^{3} } < 0\end{array}$

**Final answer:** **The area of 1 square unit is a maximum area as the gradient **$\frac{dA}{dθ}$** goes from positive to negative**

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** For an attempt to find the value of $\frac{dA}{dθ}$ either side of $θ=2$.
> 
> **A1: **For correctly showing that the gradient goes from positive to negative from left of $θ=2$ to right of $θ=2$ (no formal conclusion sentence needed).

parts.problemMd:
A curve is given by $y = ln ( 1 + x^{4} )$.

Use calculus to find the approximate change in $y$ as $x$ increases from $-1$ to $-1+k$ where $k$ is small.
parts.solutionMd:
> *In general, the approximate change in *$y$* as *$x$* increases from *$a$* to *$a+h$* where *$h$* is small is *$\frac{dy}{dx}\timesh$* where *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* is at *$x=a$

> *Substitute *$a=-1$* and *$h=k$* into the expression above*

$\frac{dy}{dx}\timesk$* where *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* is at *$x=-1$

> *Find *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* using the chain rule, *$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\frac{du}{dx}$* where *$u=1+x^{4}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}y = & ln u u = 1 + x^{4} \\ \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} u} & = & \frac{1}{u} \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 4 x ^{3} \end{array}$

> *This gives*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = \frac{1}{u} \\times 4 x^{3} \\ = \frac{1}{1 + x^{4} } \\times 4 x^{3} \\ = \frac{4 x^{3}}{1 + x^{4} } \end{gathered}$

**[M1 A1]**

> *Substitute *$x=-1$* into *$\frac{dy}{dx}$

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = & \frac{4 ( - 1 ) ^{3} }{1 + ( - 1 ) ^{4}} = - 2\end{array}$

**[M1]**

> *Substitute *$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} \end{gathered} = - 2$* into *$\frac{dy}{dx}\timesk$

$-2k$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1: **For having $\frac{1}{1+x^{4}}$ in your expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
> 
> **A1: **For the fully correct expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
> 
> **M1:** For substituting $x=-1$ into your expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
> 
> **A1: **For $-2k$ as the final answer.

parts.problemMd:
In this question, all lengths are in centimetres.

![q11-2025-specimen-paper-2-cie-igcse-additional-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-further-maths-additional-maths-25/calculus/differentiation/assets/002-q11-2025-specimen-paper-2-cie-igcse-additional-m.png)

The diagram shows a cone of base radius $x$, height $y$ and sloping edge $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$. The volume of the cone is $10π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$.

Show that the curved surface area, $S$, of the cone is given by $S=\frac{π\sqrt{x^{6}+900}}{x}$.
parts.solutionMd:
*We know that the curved surface area of a cone, *$S$*, is *$πrl$*.*
 $r$* in this case is actually *$x$* and the slant height *$l$* is given as *$\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$*. But the expression given for the curved surface are is in terms of *$x$* only.* 
*Therefore we need to find an expression for *$y$* in terms of *$x$*.*

> *We are given a value for the volume, '*$10π$*'. Therefore equate *$10π$* to the formula for volume of a cone in terms of the radius *$x$* and height *$y$*.*

$10π=\frac{1}{3}πx^{2}y$

> *Rearrange to get an expression for *$y$* in terms of *$x$*.*

$\begin{gathered} y = \frac{10 \pi }{1 \frac{1}{3} \pi x^{2}} \\ = \frac{30}{x^{2}} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Now substitute *$x=r$* and *$l=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$* where *$y=\frac{30}{x^{2}}$* into *$S=πrl$*.*

$S = pi x \sqrt{x ^{2} + ( \frac{30}{x} ^{2} ) ^{2} }$

**[1]**

> *This is starting to approach something that looks like the final answer. To get to the final answer, start by expanding the bracket inside the square root.*

$S=πx\sqrt{x^{2}+\frac{900}{x^{4}}}$

> *Note that there's no fraction inside the square root of the final answer. Rewrite '*$x^{2}+\frac{900}{x^{4}}$*' as a single fraction.*

$S=πx\sqrt{\frac{x^{6}+900}{x^{4}}}$

> *Now take the square root of the denominator of the fraction.*

$S=πx\frac{\sqrt{x^{6}+900}}{x^{2}}$

> *Cancel the *$x$* and the *$x^{2}$*.*

`S = pi / x (sqrt( x ^ 6 + 900 ))/(/ x ^2 )`

$S=\frac{π\sqrt{x^{6}+900}}{x}$**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In this question, all lengths are in centimetres.

The diagram shows a cone of base radius x, height y and sloping edge √(x² + y²). The volume of the cone is 10π cm³.

Show that the curved surface area, S, of the cone is given by S = (π√(x^6 + 900))/x.

Given that $x$ can vary and that $S$ has a minimum value, find the value of $x$ for which $S$ is a minimum.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We will need to differentiate *$S$* and then equate the derivative to 0 to find the minimum value of *$x$*. *
*As differentiation will be involved, rewrite the square root as a fractional power.*

$S = \frac{pi \sqrt{x^{6} + 900}}{x} = \frac{pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{1} half}{x}$

> *To differentiate *$S$* we need to use the quotient rule.*

`S = (pi ( x ^ 6 + 900 ) ^ 1 half )/(x) = u / v , where u = pi ( x ^ 6 + 900 ) ^ 1 half and v = x`

> *From here we need to find *$\frac{du}{dx}$* and *$\frac{dv}{dx}$*. However we need to use the chain rule to find *$\frac{du}{dx}$*.*

`u = pi ( x ^ 6 + 900 ) ^ 1 half , let u = pi w ^ 1 half and w = x ^ 6 + 900`

> *Now differentiate **u** and **w.*

$\frac{du}{dw}=π\times\frac{1}{2}w^{-\frac{1}{2}},\frac{dw}{dx}=6x^{5}$

> *And apply the chain rule, in this case *$\frac{du}{dx}=\frac{du}{dw}\times\frac{dw}{dx}$*.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = \pi 1 \frac{1}{2} w^{- 1 \frac{1}{2}} \\times 6 x^{5 \\ = \pi 1 \frac{1}{2} ( x^{6} + 900 )^{-1} \frac{1}{2}} \\times 6 x^{5} \end{gathered}$

** **$\begin{gathered} \pi 1 \frac{1}{2} ( x^{6 + 900 )^{-1} \frac{1}{2}} \end{gathered}$** ****[1]**

$\begin{gathered} = 3 \pi x^{5 ( x^{6} + 900 )^{-1} \frac{1}{2}} \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Now we are ready to go back to *$S=\frac{u}{v}$* where *$u=π\sqrt{x^{6}+900}$* and *$v=x$*.*

`| u = pi ( x ^ 6 + 900 ) ^ 1 half and v = x | | ( d u)/( d x) | = 3 pi x ^ 5 ( x ^ 6 + 900 ) ^ negative 1 half ( d v)/( d x) = 1 | |`

> *Apply the quotient rule, *$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{v\frac{du}{dx}-u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^{2}}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} S}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{x ( 3 pi x^{5} ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} ) - pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{1} half}{x ^{2} }$

**[1]**

> *At the minimum value of S, *$\frac{dS}{dx}=0$*, so equate this derivative to 0.*

$\frac{x ( 3 pi x^{5} ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} ) - pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{1} half}{x ^{2} } = 0$

> *Solve - start by multiplying by the denominator, *$x^{2}$*.*

$x ( 3 pi x^{5} ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} ) - pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{1} \text{half} = 0$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$3 pi x^{6} ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} - pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) ^{1} \text{half} = 0$

> *Remove the negative power.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{3 \pi x^{6}{( x^{6} + 900 )^{1} \frac{1}{2}} } - \pi ( x^{6 + 900 )^{1} \frac{1}{2}} & = 0 \\ \text{or} \frac{3 \pi x^{6} }{ \sqrt{x^{6} + 900} } - \pi \sqrt{x^{6} + 900} & = 0 \end{gathered}$

> *Multiply by *$\sqrt{x^{6}+900}$*.*

$3 pi x^{6} - pi ( x^{6} + 900 ) = 0$

> *Divide by *$π$* and complete the solution.*

$\begin{array}{cc}3 x^{6} - ( x^{6} + 900 ) & = 0 \\ 3 x^{6} - x^{6} - 900 & = 0 \\ 2 x^{6} & = 900 \\ x^{6} & = 450\end{array}$

** **`x = sqrt index 6 of 450 = 2 . 768229457 . . . or 2 . 77 stretchy ( 3 s. f. stretchy )`  **[1] **
**Note that **$x$** is a length therefore **`x not equal to negative root index 6 of 450`

parts.problemMd: Variables $x$ and $y$ are such that $y=\frac{e^{3x}\mathrm{sin}x}{x^{2}}$ .Use differentiation to find the approximate change in $y$as $x$ increases from $0.5\mathrm{to}0.5+h$, where $h$is small.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Recall that*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( e^{3} x ) = 3 e^{3} x$

**[1]**

> *Use the product rule to differentiate the numerator and then apply the quotient rule.*

> *When you differentiate the numerator using the product rule you will get*

$e^{3x}\mathrm{cos}x+3e^{3x}\mathrm{sin}x$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( \frac{e^{3} x \text{sin} x}{x ^{2} } ) = \frac{x ^{2} ( e^{3} x \text{cos} x + 3 e^{3} x \text{sin} x ) - 2 x ( e^{3} x \text{sin} x ) }{ ( x ^{2} ) ^{2} }$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( \frac{e^{3} x \text{sin} x}{x ^{2} } ) = \frac{x ^{2} e^{3} x \text{cos} x + 3 x ^{2} e^{3} x \text{sin} x - 2 x e^{3} x \text{sin} x}{x^{4}}$

**[1]**

> *Evaluate the derivative above when *$x=0.5$* using the radian mode on your calculator.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( \frac{e^{3} x \text{sin} x}{x ^{2} } ) = 7.13766...$

**[1]**

> *As *$h$* is small, use *$"\mathrm{Change} \mathrm{in}y=\mathrm{Gradient}\times\mathrm{Change} \mathrm{in}x"$*.*

$7.14\timesh$

**Approximate change in **$y$** is**$7.14h$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
In this question all lengths are in centimetres. The volume, $V$, of a cone of height $h$ and base radius $r$ is given by $V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$

![q11-0606-s20-qp-23-additional-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-further-maths-additional-maths-25/calculus/differentiation/assets/003-q11-0606-s20-qp-23-additional-maths.png)

The diagram shows a large hollow cone from which a smaller cone of height 180 and base radius 90 has been removed. The remainder has been fitted with a circular base of radius 90 to form a container for water. The depth of water in the container is w and the surface of the water is a circle of radius $R$.

Find an expression for $R$ in terms of $w$ and show that the volume $V$ of the water in the container is given by $V = \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{12} ( w + 180 )^{3} - 486000 \mathrm{\pi }$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We actually need to work with a 'third' cone - formed from the larger hollow cone described in the question but with a height that is determined by the (higher) water level. All three cones are similar and since the radius of the smaller cone is half its own height, the radius of the 'third' cone will be half its own height too.*

$\text{therefore} R = \frac{1}{2} ( w + 180 )$

**[1]**

> *The volume of the water can be found by subtracting the volume of the smaller cone from that of the 'third' cone.*

$V = 1 \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 1 \frac{1}{2} ( w + 180 ) )^{2} ( w + 180 ) - 1 \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 90 )^{2} ( 180 )$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{gathered} V = 1 \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{2} ( w + 180 )^{2} ( w + 180 ) - 1 \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 90 )^{2} ( 180 ) \\ V = ( 1 \frac{1}{3} ) ( 1 \frac{1}{4} ) \mathrm{\pi } ( w + 180 )^{3} - 486000 \mathrm{\pi } \end{gathered}$

$V=\frac{π}{12}(w+180)^{3}-486000π$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The diagram shows a large hollow cone from which a smaller cone of height 180 and base radius 90 has been removed. The remainder has been fitted with a circular base of radius 90 to form a container for water. The depth of water in the container is w and the surface of the water is a circle of radius R.

Find an expression for R in terms of w and show that the volume V of the water in the container is given by V = (π/12)(w + 180)³ - 486000π.

Water is poured into the container at a rate of $10000\mathrm{cm}^{3}s^{-1}$. Find the rate at which the depth of the water is increasing when $w=10$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *This is a connected rates of change question, we will need to use chain rule.  At time *$t$*,*

$\frac{dw}{dt}=\frac{dw}{dV}\times\frac{dV}{dt}$

> *The rate at which the volume (*$V$*) is changing with respect to the height of the water (*$w$*) is*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} V}{ \mathrm{d} w} = 3 \frac{pi}{12} ( w + 180 ) ^{2}$

**[1]**

> *We require *$\frac{dw}{dV}$*.*

> $\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} V} = \frac{1}{ \frac{\mathrm{\pi }}{4} ( w + 180 )^{2}}$*   *

> *We know the rate at which water is poured into the container with respect to time.*

$\frac{dV}{dt}=10000$

> *Apply chain rule.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{\frac{pi}{4} ( w + 180 ) ^{2} } \times 10000$

**[1]**

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} t} = \frac{40000}{ \mathrm{\pi } ( w + 180 )^{2}}$

> *When *$w=10$*,*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} t} = \frac{40000}{ \mathrm{\pi } ( 10 + 180 )^{2}}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify and evaluate.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} t} = \frac{40000}{ \mathrm{\pi } ( 190 )^{2}}$
$\frac{ \mathrm{d} w}{ \mathrm{d} t} = 0.3526...$

$\frac{dw}{dt}=0.353\mathrm{cm}s^{-1}(3s.f.)$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A curve has equation $y = \frac{ln ( 3 x ^{2} - 5 ) }{2 x + 1} \text{for} 3 x ^{2} > 5$

Find the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $x=\sqrt{2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate the equation using quotient rule and chain rule.*

> $u = ln ( 3 x ^{2} - 5 )$*    *$v=2x+1$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( \frac{1}{3 x ^{2} - 5} ) \times 6 x$*    *$\frac{dv}{dx}=2$

**correct **$\frac{du}{dx}$**[1]**

> *Use quotient rule, *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( v ) ( \frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} ) - ( u ) ( \frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} ) }{v ^{2} }$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{ ( ( 2 x + 1 ) ( \frac{6 x}{3 x ^{2} - 5} ) ) - ( 2 ) ( ln ( 3 x ^{2} - 5 ) ) }{ ( 2 x + 1 ) ^{2} }$

** ****quotient rule**** [1]**
** ****all terms correct except **$\frac{6x}{3x^{2}-5}$** [1]**

> *When *$x=\sqrt{2}$*,*

$y = \frac{\ln ( 1 )}{2 \sqrt{2} + 1}$

> $ln ( 1 ) = 0$*, therefore when *$x=\sqrt{2}$*,*

$y=0$

**[1]**

> *Substitute *$x=\sqrt{2}$* into *$\frac{dy}{dx}$* to find the gradient of the curve at this point.*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} & = \frac{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 ) ( \frac{6 \sqrt{2} }{3 ( \sqrt{2} )^{2} - 5} ) - 2 \ln ( 3 ( \sqrt{2} )^{2} - 5 )}{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 )^{2}} \\ \\ = \frac{( \frac{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 ) ( 6 \sqrt{2} )}{1} ) - 2 \ln ( 1 )}{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 )^{2}} \\ \\ = \frac{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 ) ( 6 \sqrt{2} )}{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 )^{2}} \\ \\ = \frac{6 \sqrt{2} }{2 \sqrt{2} + 1} \end{gathered}$

> *Take the negative reciprocal to find the gradient of the normal.*

$\text{gradient} ( \text{normal} ) = - \frac{2 \sqrt{2} + 1}{6 \sqrt{2} }$

> *Substitute this gradient and the point *$( \sqrt{2} , 0 )$* into the equation of line, *$y - y_{1} = m \left(x - x_{1}\right)$*.*

$\begin{gathered} y - 0 & = - \frac{2 \sqrt{2} + 1}{6 \sqrt{2} } ( x - \sqrt{2} ) \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

$\begin{gathered} y = - \frac{( 2 \sqrt{2} + 1 ) ( x - \sqrt{2} )}{6 \sqrt{2} } \\ \\ y = - 0.451 184... x + 0.638 071... \end{gathered}$

$y=-0.451x+0.638(3s.f.)$* ***[1]**

At the point where x space equals space square root of 2:

parts.problemMd:
![q9-0606-w20-qp-23-additional-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-further-maths-additional-maths-25/calculus/differentiation/assets/004-q9-0606-w20-qp-23-additional-maths.png)

The rectangle $ABCDE$ represents a ploughed field where $AB=300m$ and $AE=400m$. Joseph needs to walk from $A$ to $D$ in the least possible time. He can walk at $0.9\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ on the ploughed field and at $1.5\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ on any part of the path $BCD$ along the edge of the field. He walks from $A$ to $C$ and then from $C$ to $D$. The distance $BC=xm$.

Find, in terms of $x$, the total time, $Ts$, Joseph takes for the journey.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use Pythagoras' Theorem to find the length **AC **in terms of** *$x$*.*

$\begin{array}{ccc}A C ^{2} & = & 300 ^{2} + x ^{2} \\ A C & = & \sqrt{90 000 + x ^{2} }\end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Use *$"\mathrm{av}.\mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{time}}"$*(rearranged) to find the time to walk **AC** (speed on the ploughed field).*

$\mathrm{Time} \mathrm{for}AC=\frac{\sqrt{90000+x^{2}}}{0.9}=\frac{10}{9}\sqrt{90000+x^{2}}$

**[1]**

> *Similarly for **CD** (speed on the path),*

$Time \text{for} C D = \frac{400 - x}{1.5} = \frac{2 ( 400 - x ) }{3}$

> *Add the times together to find the total time, **T**.*

$T = \frac{10}{9} \sqrt{90 000 + x ^{2} } + \frac{2 ( 400 - x ) }{3}$

> $T=\frac{6(400-x)+10\sqrt{90000+x^{2}}}{9}$* [1] *
*Equivalent expressions are acceptable*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The rectangle ABCDE represents a ploughed field where AB = 300 m and AE = 400 m. Joseph needs to walk from A to D in the least possible time. He can walk at 0.9 ms⁻¹ on the ploughed field and at 1.5 ms⁻¹ on any part of the path BCD along the edge of the field. He walks from A to C and then from C to D. The distance BC = x m.

$T = \frac{10}{9} \sqrt{90 000 + x ^{2} } + \frac{2 ( 400 - x ) }{3}$

Given that $x$ can vary, find the value of $x$ for which $T$ is a minimum and hence find the minimum value of $T$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Rewrite **T **to make it easier to differentiate.*

$T = \frac{2}{9} ( 1200 - 3 x + 5 ( x ^{2} + 90 000 ) ^{1} \text{half} )$

> $\frac{2}{9}$* is a constant, differentiate using chain rule for *$( x ^{2} + 90 000 ) ^{1} \text{half}$*.*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} T}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{2}{9} ( - 3 + \frac{5}{2} ( x ^{2} + 90 000 ) ^{ - } \frac{1}{2} \times 2 x )$
$\frac{ \mathrm{d} T}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \frac{2}{9} ( \frac{5 x}{\sqrt{x ^{2} + 90 000}} - 3 )$

**for correct differentiation of **$( x ^{2} + 90 000 ) ^{1} \text{half}$** ****[1]**

**all correct ****[1]**

> *We are asked to find the minimum value, this is when *$\frac{dT}{dx}=0$*.*

$\frac{2}{9} ( \frac{5 x}{\sqrt{x ^{2} + 90 000}} - 3 ) = 0$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve for *$x$*.*

$\begin{array}{ccc}\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{x ^{2} + 90 000}} & = 3 \\ 5 x & = & 3 \sqrt{x ^{2} + 90 000}\end{array}$

> *Square both sides.*

$\begin{array}{ccc}25 x ^{2} & = & 9 ( x ^{2} + 90 000 ) \\ 16 x ^{2} & = & 810 000 \\ x ^{2} & = 50625 \\ x = & \pm 225\end{array}$

**[1]**

> *As *$x$* is a distance, it can only take a positive value.*

$\begin{array}{rcl} x = 225 \end{array}$

**[1]**

*Substitute *$x=225$ *into the equation for **T**.*

$T = \frac{2}{9} ( 1200 - 3 \times 225 + 5 \sqrt{225 ^{2} + 90 000} )$
T equals 1600 over 3

**The minimum value of **$T$** is **$\frac{1600}{3}$**(seconds)**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
A curve has the equation $y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$.

Find and factorise an expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate *$y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$* using the chain rule*

> *i.e. substitute *$y=e^{u}$* and *$u=4x-x^{2}$* into *$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\times\frac{du}{dx}$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = \mathrm{e} ^{u} \times ( 4 - 2 x )$

**[M1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for attempting to use the chain rule.

> *Substitute back in *$u=4x-x^{2}$* to get the first derivative in *$x$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = ( 4 - 2 x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

> *Factorise out 2 from the first bracket*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Hence find $\int \frac{( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x} }{ \mathrm{e}^{x^{2}} } \mathrm{d} x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The first derivative from part (a) says that if *$y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$* then*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

> *Reverse the process to go from the first derivative back to the equation of the curve*

$\text{integral} 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} ) \mathrm{d} x = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} ) + c$

> *The integral in the question is almost the same as this, but needs rearranging first*

$\begin{gathered} \int \frac{( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x} }{ \mathrm{e}^{x^{2}} } \mathrm{d} x & = \int ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x - x^{2}} \mathrm{d} x \\ = 1 \frac{1}{2} \int 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x - x^{2}} \mathrm{d} x \end{gathered}$

> *Now substitute the reversed integral from above into the right-hand side here*

$\begin{gathered} \int \frac{( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x} }{ \mathrm{e}^{x^{2}} } \mathrm{d} x & = 1 \frac{1}{2} [ \mathrm{e}^{( 4 x - x^{2} )} + c ] \end{gathered}$

> *Expand (you can rename the unknown constant *$\frac{1}{2}c$* as *$c$* again)*

$\begin{gathered} \int \frac{( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e}^{4 x} }{ \mathrm{e}^{x^{2}} } \mathrm{d} x & = 1 \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{e}^{( 4 x - x^{2} )} + c \end{gathered}$

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** For at least $\frac{1}{2}e^{4x-x^{2}}$ (may not have $+c$).
> 
> **B1:** For $\frac{1}{2}e^{4x-x^{2}}+c$ (must have$+c$).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always add $+c$ to your answers to indefinite integrals, otherwise you will lose a mark!

parts.problemMd:
Show that the second derivative of the curve $y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$ satisfies the relationship

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = ( p + q x + r x ^{2} ) y$

where $p$, $q$ and $r$ are constants to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} y}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$* again to get *$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$* but this time using the product rule *$\frac{du}{dx}v+u\frac{dv}{dx}$

> *First find the derivatives of *$u = 2 ( 2 - x ) = 4 - 2 x$* and *$v = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$*  (note that *$\frac{dv}{dx}$*is the answer to part (a))*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} u}{ \mathrm{d} x} = - 2$
$\frac{ \mathrm{d} v}{ \mathrm{d} x} = 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

> *Then substitute these into *$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\frac{du}{dx}v+u\frac{dv}{dx}$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = ( - 2 ) \times \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} ) + ( 4 - 2 x ) \times [ 2 ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} ) ]$

**[M1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for attempting to use the product rule.

> *Simplify*

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = - 2 \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} ) + 4 ( 2 - x ) ( 2 - x ) \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This mark is for the correct result after using the product rule (it can be unsimplified and messy).

> *Factorise out *$\mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$* because the answer must be written in the form *$( p + q x + r x ^{2} ) y$* and *$y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = [ - 2 + 4 ( 2 - x ) ( 2 - x ) ] \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

**[M1]**

> *Expand and simplify inside the brackets*

$\begin{gathered} \frac{ \mathrm{d}^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x^{2}} & = ( - 2 + 4 ( 4 - 4 x + x^{2} ) ) \mathrm{e}^{( 4 x - x^{2} )} \\ = ( - 2 + 16 - 16 x + 4 x^{2} ) \mathrm{e}^{( 4 \mathrm{x} - \mathrm{x}^{2} )} \\ = ( 14 - 16 x + 4 x^{2} ) \mathrm{e}^{( 4 x - x^{2} )} \end{gathered}$

> *The result is meant to have the form *$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = ( p + q x + r x ^{2} ) y$

> *This is true, as *$y = \mathrm{e} ^{open} \text{parentheses} 4 x - x ^{2} )$

$\frac{ \mathrm{d} ^{2} y}{ \mathrm{d} x ^{2} } = ( 14 - 16 x + 4 x ^{2} ) y$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
Giving your answer in its simplest form, find the exact value of

$integral_{0}^{4} \frac{10}{5 x + 2} d x$
parts.solutionMd:

> *Integrate the fraction using reverse chain rule.*

$= 10 [ \begin{gathered} 1 \frac{1}{5} \ln ( 5 x + 2 ) \end{gathered} ]_{ 0}^{ 4}$

$k\timesln(5x+2)$**[1]**

$= 10 \\times 1 \frac{1}{5} [ \begin{gathered} \ln ( 5 x + 2 ) \end{gathered} ]_{ 0}^{ 4}$

$= 2 [ \begin{gathered} \ln ( 5 x + 2 ) \end{gathered} ]_{ 0}^{ 4}$

**[1]**

**[1]**

$2\mathrm{ln}11$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: $integral_{0}^{ln} 2 ( \mathrm{e} ^{4} x + 2 ) ^{2} \mathrm{d} x$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the law of logarithms, *$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$*.*

$\begin{gathered} \int_{0}^{\ln 2} ( \mathrm{e}^{4 x + 2} )^{2} \mathrm{d} x & = \int_{0}^{\ln 2} ( \mathrm{e}^{2 ( 4 x + 2 )} ) \mathrm{d} x \\ = \int_{0}^{\ln 2} \mathrm{e}^{8 x + 4} \mathrm{d} x \end{gathered}$

**[1]**

> *Integrate.*

$= [ \begin{gathered} \frac{1}{8} \mathrm{e}^{8 x + 4} \end{gathered} ]_{ 0}^{ \ln 2}$

**[1]**

> *Apply the limits.*

$=\frac{1}{8}e^{8\mathrm{ln}2+4}-\frac{1}{8}e^{4}$

> *Factorise *$\frac{1}{8}$*.*

$= \frac{1}{8} ( \mathrm{e} ^{8} ln 2 + 4 - \mathrm{e} ^{4} )$

**[1]**

> *Rewrite the first exponential term as a product of 2 terms.*

$= \frac{1}{8} ( \mathrm{e} ^{8} ln 2 \times \mathrm{e} ^{4} - \mathrm{e} ^{4} )$

$= \frac{1}{8} ( \mathrm{e} ^{ } ln 2^{8} \times \mathrm{e} ^{4} - \mathrm{e} ^{4} )$

**[1]**

> *The exponential and natural log are inverses so cancel each other out.*

$= \frac{1}{8} ( 256 \mathrm{e} ^{4} - \mathrm{e} ^{4} )$

> *Factorise *$e^{4}$*.*

$= \frac{1}{8} \mathrm{e} ^{4} ( 256 - 1 )$

$=\frac{255}{8}e^{4}$

$\frac{255}{8}e^{4}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Find $\frac{ \mathrm{d} }{ \mathrm{d} x} ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}}$and hence evaluate the area enclosed by the curve $y=x\sqrt{16-x^{2}}$ and the lines $y=0,x=1\mathrm{and}x=3$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate using the chain rule. *

$\begin{gathered} \frac{d}{d x} ( 16 - x^{2} )^{ \frac{3}{2} } & = \frac{3}{2} ( 16 - x^{2} )^{1 \frac{1}{2}} \\times ( - 2 x ) \\ = - 3 x ( 16 - x^{2} )^{1 \frac{1}{2}} \end{gathered}$

** ****attempt at chain rule ****[1]**
** ****fully correct**** [1]**

> *The area required is given by the integral*

$integral_{1}^{3} x ( 16 - x ^{2} ) ^{1} \text{half} d x$

$\begin{gathered} \int_{1}^{3} x ( 16 - x^{2} )^{1 \frac{1}{2}} d x & = - 1 \frac{1}{3} \int_{1}^{3} x ( 16 - x^{2} )^{1 \frac{1}{2}} d x \\ = - 1 \frac{1}{3} [ ( 16 - x^{2} )^{ \frac{3}{2} } ]_{1}^{3} \end{gathered}$

$( - \frac{1}{3} ( 16 - 3 ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} ) - ( - \frac{1}{3} ( 16 - 1 ^{2} ) ^{\frac{3}{2}} )$

**Area is **$13.2\mathrm{units}^{2}$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
(a)

$\text{integral} \frac{1}{open} \text{parentheses} 7 x + 4 ) ^{2} \mathrm{d} x$

> *Write it in the form *$( a x + b ) ^{n}$* using negative indices*

$\text{integral} ( 7 x + 4 ) ^{ - } 2 \mathrm{d} x$

> *Use the rule *$\text{integral} ( a x + b ) ^{n} \mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{a} \times \frac{1}{n + 1} ( a x + b ) ^{n} + 1 + c$

$\text{integral} ( 7 x + 4 ) ^{ - } 2 \mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{7} \times \frac{1}{ - 2 + 1} ( 7 x + 4 ) ^{ - } 2 + 1 + c$

> *Simplify*

$\begin{gathered} = \frac{1}{7} \\times \frac{1}{- 1} ( 7 x + 4 )^{- 1} + c \\ = - \frac{1}{7} ( 7 x + 4 )^{- 1} + c \end{gathered}$

> *Present the final answer (including *$+c$*)*

$\begin{array}{ccc} \text{integral} ( 7 x + 4 ) ^{ - } 2 \mathrm{d} x & = & - \frac{1}{7} ( 7 x + 4 ) ^{ - } 1 + c\end{array}$

**[B2]**

(b)

$\text{integral} \frac{1}{7 x + 4} \mathrm{d} x$

> *Use the rule *$\text{integral} \frac{1}{a x + b} \mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{a} ln \mid a x + b \mid + c$


$\text{integral} \frac{1}{7 x + 4} \mathrm{d} x = \frac{1}{7} ln \mid 7 x + 4 \mid + c$
